Messages.Author: Rob Grau
Messages.Body:
Quick Summary of points as I see them:

From the "Something needs to be done about Life Boon" camp:

1. It's a master card that arbitraily reassigns victory points in the
game.
Counterpoint: So? You don't have to like it. You're not going to win the
tournament by removing yourself from it.

2. Pool Swing from self oust aspect is unbalancing. (Saved methuselah
has at least 6 pool, usually 10+)
Counterpoint: A robust tournament winning deck should be able to
overcome a prey with more than 30 pool, or perhaps some decks will have
counters for this so it won't matter.

3. Sign of abused card: Included in most tournament "winning" decks. (at
least in the Southeast US)
Counterpoint: Small sample size, why isn't it included in winning decks
all over the world?

4. Can be abused universally in all deck types.
Counterpoint: Master slots too valuable to seriously consider adding LB
to all decks, particularly combat decks.

From the "There isn't a solid reason to change Life Boon" camp:

1. There are better master cards to use out there.
Counterpoint: Like what? Even Minion Tap doesn't necessarily give you a
VP. You should include at least a couple in your deck.

2. 1VP at a time is not a method to win tournaments.
Counterpoint: True, but an _extra_ VP every other game can nudge a deck
into the finals, where an extra VP can usually mean at least second
place.

3. You have to wait for the situation to arise, I mean, you actively try
to oust your prey, but your grandpredator has to be strong for your
predator to be ousted.
Counterpoint: The situation arises more often than not. It's really not
that hard to pull off.

4. Maybe it _is_ cheesy and boring, but the same has been said about
Majesty.
Counterpoint: Well, at least you admit there is a problem. (This isn't
really a debatable point, either the person is debating the other points
or you hear this)

------------
Well, I'm sure this list isn't all inclusive, but it should keep the
debate rolling, feel free to add or subtract from the list.

Personally, I don't see a problem with the card. You are taking yourself
out of the game preventing the accumulation of any other victory points.
True, it is a way to get an early out and potentially win the game but,
you will have already had to win victory points (and sufficient number)
to win the game.

I have heard more bitching from friends about misdirections and force of
will. The only way to stop misdirection is with a sudden reversal
(ignoring a wake, cause stealth becomes an issue, and additional
predator vamps can get past a one wake already used up), and that could be
a game winner as well, almost always giving a victory point if well-played
and timed.

Force of Will (one of my favorite cards) can be used after you force your
prey to tap out due to other bleeds, and if no wake is available, is
usually always successful. Sure, you go to torpor, but it is a small price
to gain two actions, 6 pool, and a VP.

Cheese is in the eye of the beholder, and any card can be annoying if
performed enough times, be it Force, misdirection, combat ends
(especially with untap), any minion with +1 stealth to all actions...

In an attempt to compile a neutral list of points, I may have unintentionally
weakened the argument by saying "or blah, blah, blah." But I think this is a
more reasonable line of debate than the "So?" counterpoint I proposed.

> I mean, you're right, they should be
> able to handle pool gain decks. But that doesn't mean it's a good thing
> to support a tactic that capriciously hands an arbitrarily chosen player
> 10+ pool just for being in the right place at the right time.

A good thing(TM) and unbalancing are different ideas. I think the Direct
Intervention debate made a clear distinction between the two.

> In fact,
> it's not even entirely being in the right place at the right time but
> also a matter of being *ineffective* at protecting yourself from your
> preditor which contributes to your sudden windfall.

Ineffective deck type or not, the fact remains that you gain pool as if you
had ousted two methuselahs. The argument I proposed does not agrue if the
life boon beneficiary deserves the pool but rather what happens when the
power shift occurs. It is a valid argument to say that "it is not
unreasonable to expect a deck to gain 12 pool in a game, therefore a good
deck should be able to deal with it" The part about the deck being
ineffective may work against the case for changing Life Boon because a bad
deck will not be gaining pool otherwise.

I guess you're going to have to clarify what definition you're using
for the term "unbalancing". I've heard it used for cards which were not
adequately play-balance but that sure didn't sound like how you used it
in the text I quoted above. It _sounded_ like you meant that the effect
of the card unbalanced the game it was used in - i.e., granted one
Methuselah an arbitrary advantage over another. This it certainly does.
And if the counterpoint you gave was intended to communicate that such
"imbalance" was not automatically a "bad thing" - which is the idea
suggested by the original point - it failed to do so.

to players who haven't done anything at all to deserve them can be seen as
anything *but* a "bad thing". The only question is whether it's a bad
enough thing to worry about and/or whether the card does anything "good"
to merit retaining it in its current form. (Granted that just the additional
card variety and the lack of one more piece of errata or another card
banning are somewhat good in and of themselves.)

Fred

Messages.Author: legb...@my-deja.com
Messages.Body:
i think it's nice that we're having a debate about life boon and i hope
this is not just a bit of window-dressing prior to an already-decided-
upon RT ruling. Overall i'm with my esteemed colleague the hated Coupe
[beneath whose Iron Heel the Kindred of Central England Nightly Groan] on
this. However, i want to comment separately on some theoretical issues
[but only briefly, because i am a methuselah of very little brain], on
what the card actually does for the game [positive aspects if you like],
and to offer an opinion about why it seems to be a problem in SE USA, and
not elsewhere.

THEORETICAL STUFF
i think it's dangerous territory to state that Life Boon is bad because
it arbitrarily gives people something for nothing. That argument would
lead to fixes/bans for Malkavian Game and Prank and Game of Malkav, and
for that matter the whole concept of shuffling one's deck.

GOOD STUFF
Life Boon makes combat decks viable at tournament level, because a combat
deck can use it to get a VP out of the normal tactic of shafting its
predator. And Life Boon IS used by thoughtful and judicious players like
James Coupe to control the table, and by creative but crazy players like
Philippe Richer to contrive mad schemes of winning by sequentially
ousting their predators.

OPINIONATED STUFF
Ultra-fast bleed decks [Boo!] and combat decks [Hoorah!] seem to be much
more common in the colonies than over here. i must admit that in such an
environment pretty much any deck would need a life boon. Here ultra-fast
bleed is somewhat in abeyance because we have a lot of massive bleed/
vote/runaway decks and a lot of really fierce multi-action combat decks
too. If we were theoretically-minded over here we might be groaning about
how broken Minion Tap, Golconda, Dramatic Upheaval and Kindred
Restructure are, but we aren't, twice.

EMOLLIENT COMPROMISING STUFF AT THE END
Can i suggest a prize for the top 20 or so players in the VEKN ratings
that wouldn't cost anybody anything to buy or post and would probably be
reasonably popular with everyone? Couldn't they have a vote on any
proposed fix to a card in future? i suggest that LSJ is ex officio Inner
Circle Member, Robert Goudie Justicar, whoever comes top is Prince and
everybody else is a primogen.

I think we should consider the mechanics of such a restriction. You could
also support the errata "you may not play Life Boon." That is simple and
elegant too, but most people dislike banning cards.

Consider how the solution is similar to banning. Currently, the reasons to
Life Boon your prey are small. If you choose to reduce your prey to zero
pool, why would you life boon them? That does not make sense. I can see
another effect ousting your prey, and there are bound to be a very small
number of good reasons to LB your prey. The errata "you may not play Life
Boon on your predator" eliminates another target. Likewise, there should be
a set of reasons to LB your predator that does not involve the self oust VP,

(or a variant of the "self oust": I have one pool, you'll kill me soon!)
This means that LB has little utility in a game with less than 4
methuselahs. What happens with 3 players when you need to LB your predator
to keep your prey from getting six pool, and the victory point to go with
it? Why is it fair to say that you can use this effect when there are 4
people in the game but not 3? I think this significantly alters the original

intent of Life Boon. This fix also does not address Ben Peal's objection
that it gives the methuselah too much power in the game, it just tries to
limit the situations in which it occurs.

Since I object to the errata, I'll propose a different fix: "You may give up

to half of your current pool (round down) to the Methuselah with zero pool."

This prevents a self oust situation, and limits abuses by giving away 90% of

your pool. If you only had two pool to start with, I would argue that your
position was not very strong anyway.

This is a fairly simple fix, like the others proposed.

This works to limit the unbalancing effect of giving a lot of pool to any
methuselah and letting the game take a significantly new course. It does not

solve this problem. If you are running a bloat deck and have 15 pool (30 or
more total) to give away, then that's more a product of the bloat deck more
than the life boon. Using Succubus Club would lead to an equally bad
situation with that much pool.

A caveat: I haven't even playtested this. It might have some real pitfalls.
I just think it addresses the issues better than "don't play on your
predator."

Thanks,

I agree that this is one way to interpret the card text, but I do not
think that Life Boon is similar in any way to either Vast Wealth or
Horrid Reality. For both of those cards there is a very specific,
action-oriented context in which the term "first" has an obvious,
non-ambiguous meaning. That is, both cards direct the player to search
his library and select the first weapon they come across. In this case
the term "first" is completely unambiguous.

For Life Boon, I would suggest that an alternate way to read the text
implies that "wins" means over the course of the game, and not simply
from the point the Life Boon is played onward. I see no reason to prefer
one over the other, but comparing Life Boon to Horrid Reality and Vast
Wealth does not make this situation clearer simply because Life Boon
does not share the same sort of context.

If "first" is supposed to mean "next" then errata should be issued to
make misinterpretation impossible. Alternately, errata could be issued
that clarifies the scope of the term "wins" - namely, that is means over
the course of a game. This is just a recommendation for consideration by
the Rules Team if a fix for Life Boon is going to be found.

There have been examples of situations whereby you *can* play Sudden
Reversal - if they die from a pool-loss on their turn, via, say,
Antediluvian Awakening. A further possibility would be, at the end of
your grand-prey's turn, a Madness Networked bleed, such that *they* can't
play an LB (and no-one else, in this instance, can LBSO for a victory
point), or at the end of any other person's turn such that you *can*
play SR. Also, since LB is an OOT, there may be times when your
grand-prey has already played an OOT master, which you could capitalise on
(a Direct Intervention or Sudden Reversal is not entirely unknown).

A further, though entirely unworkable, possibility might involve some fun
with a Raptor deck. It would be fun to see it pulled off, at least. :)
